source_refs.note: Topic printed as 2.11.1 under 2.10, printed page 42: p-type formation. The print's 'positive-type semiconductor or N-type' is a misprint for P-type.

blocks.text: Impurity atoms with three valence electrons, such as aluminium, are added to the pure semiconductor and some of them take the place of silicon atoms in the crystal. Those silicon atoms cannot make four bonds, for lack of electrons, so holes are created in the crystal lattice, which act as positive charge carriers. This produces a positive-type (P-type) semiconductor. Electrons from an external current source can move through it, hopping into the holes, so it acts as a conductor.

blocks.prompt: Boron has the configuration 2, 3. Explain why doping silicon with boron gives a p-type semiconductor.
blocks.explanation: Boron brings only three valence electrons to a site that needs four bonds, so one bond is left without an electron: a hole. Holes act as positive charge carriers, and a semiconductor whose conduction depends on holes is p-type.

items: Trivalent impurities (Al, B) replace silicon atoms and leave bonds short, creating holes, positive carriers: a p-type semiconductor that conducts when connected to a source.
